justification: The key span is explicit: the book “records 6,140 brown trout, 288 grayling, 31 dace and nine chub”, and “one afternoon’s netting last May took four hundred-odd of them, more than the trap has held in fifteen years” — B restates exactly that, four hundred-odd dace in an afternoon against the 31 the trap has ever taken. A fails on “Since the pass opened in 2011 the trap has been emptied most mornings of the run, the counts written into a hardbacked book”: the counts start in 2011, and 1931 is only when “a mill that stopped” ceased — the weir merely “held water for” it, so even the causal claim that the weir was built to serve it is not made. C is pure invention; no span anywhere raises misidentification of chub as dace, and the two species are simply listed side by side in the tally. D inverts the arithmetic of “The first nine springs are in one hand, the rest in three others” — one keeper wrote the first nine springs and three others wrote the rest, so it is one of four, not three of four.

“39 went into the pass” and “Twelve came out at the top” fixes D: 27 of the 39 entrants never reached the top pool, so most of those that entered did not get through. A dies on the temperature split “Of the eleven that entered above ten degrees, seven got out; of the twenty-eight that entered colder, five did” — 7/11 against 5/28 is not ‘about as well’, it is roughly 64% against 18%. B is contradicted head-on by “The pools do not help. They are short, and at April flows the jet from one notch reaches the wall of the next; there is no quiet corner in them.” C misattributes the obstacle: the passage grounds the difficulty in shape, not size — “A grayling is deep through the body and carries a dorsal fin like a sail, and it does not leave the water” — and the only size argument in the text (“a dace is a small fish”) belongs to the strength explanation Kelsingham rejects.

Kelsingham states it in her own words: “They don’t find it, and they don’t find it because they don’t come up that side of the river”, with the mechanism spelled out — dace “move up in loose shoals along the margins, and the right margin is a long slack behind a shingle bar” so a fish “arrives on the far side from the entrance, thirty metres of broken water away” — and the attraction flow is too weak to reach them: “The pass releases about a quarter of a cubic metre a second; in April the river brings down nine. Four metres out from the mouth there is nothing of that quarter left to follow.” That is both halves of A. B is the explanation the text raises only to dismiss: “The explanation people reach for first is strength … Kelsingham … thinks strength has little to do with it”, and “the fall from one pool to the next about 270 millimetres” is offered as small. C invents a timing mismatch; nothing says the pass is closed at any season, and the tagged dace reached the weir within nine days. D reads shoaling as a refusal, but the text says nine of them did go in and five came out — the failure is arrival on the wrong bank, not reluctance to enter singly.

The controlled comparison is the whole point of the closing span: “A spate in February packed the lower one to the top with gravel, and it is still packed. The other, three walls further up, came through the same water clear.” ‘The same water’ explicitly holds the flood constant, so the only stated difference left to carry the outcome is height in the pass — the upper orifice stayed clear because the gravel load drops out lower down. That is C. A is precisely what ‘the same water’ rules out as the discriminator, and nothing anywhere calls the February spate unusual for this river. B misstates purpose against “so a fish could go through a wall instead of over it” — the orifices were cut for passage, not to bleed flow off the notches. D asserts a result the text never records: no fish counts at all are given for the orifices, only that one is packed and one is clear.

The text is built on a three-way contrast: trout go up freely (“a trout goes up without appearing to try”; 6,140 in the book), while dace and grayling mostly do not, and the reasons are deliberately kept separate — dace fail outside the pass (“They don’t find it … they don’t come up that side of the river”) and grayling fail inside it (“Whatever stops them is inside”, “it must swim through the jet”), with Kelsingham herself keeping them apart: “The grayling make a different case, and Kelsingham keeps them apart.” That is D. B inverts the frame — “Nobody says the pass does not work. What has taken fifteen years to become interesting is what it works for” makes the counts a starting puzzle, not support for a thesis about how passes should be judged. C shrinks the piece to its last few sentences (the 2023 orifices, the proposed second mouth), which are a coda, not the subject. A promises consequences for the river above the weir, which the text never discusses at all; the water above the pass is mentioned only as where the fish are trying to get.

“A jacket that would have ___ two pounds at half past ten goes at three for whatever coin is held out” needs the verb that takes a price as object: goods fetch a sum. ‘Fetched two pounds’ is the fixed collocation and fits the contrast with ‘goes at three for whatever coin’, both being about what the item realises. A fails because ‘earn’ takes an agent who works for the money — a jacket on a trestle does not earn; the seller might. B is the wrong sense entirely: ‘gain two pounds’ reads as acquisition or weight, not as commanding a price. C would need an investment frame (‘a return of two pounds’); ‘returned two pounds’ of a jacket at a jumble sale is not English, and in this setting it drags in the irrelevant sense of taking goods back.

“Whether the hall is worth ___ open for a last hour” is the ‘be worth + -ing’ frame, which takes a bare gerund: worth keeping open. A (‘worth keep open’) is ungrammatical; B (‘worth kept open’) is a past participle that the frame does not license and would need a passive rewrite; D (‘worth to keep open’) is the classic infinitive error — ‘worth’ never takes a to-infinitive complement. Only C leaves the sentence grammatical, and it also preserves the object relation (‘keeping the hall open’) that the surrounding clause — “is not decided on the takings” — requires.

The gap is fixed by the two spans on either side of it: “At four the prices come off … The saucers of coins go to one end of the trestle, nothing has a price after that”, and then “‘Nobody’s buying after four,’ says Irene Dunnicott … ‘They’re doing us a favour’”, with “The rest have come to carry”. Nothing is priced and nothing is bought, so the afternoon becomes a giveaway. A, C and D all keep money in the transaction and so contradict ‘nothing has a price after that’: a clearance and a markdown are sales at reduced prices, and a liquidation is a selling-off of stock — all three are still buying, which the quoted line denies outright.

The paragraph argues that lateness, not rejection, explains what is left: “the ones that arrive after two are the ones their owners have been circling all week”, and it closes “What is left at that hour is sorted by arrival time at least as much as by taste.” So the good things are on the trestles at five because they were only briefly offered — exposed for a short window rather than turned down. A inverts the argument: ‘amply offered’ would mean plentifully or generously available, which is the opposite of arriving after two. C, ‘thinly offered’, describes sparse supply across a range and cannot apply to the individual coat or tea set the sentence is about. D, ‘openly’, imports a concealment contrast the text never raises — everything on the trestles is on open display; the variable the paragraph isolates is time, not visibility.

The concession comes before the gap — “The pattern is not a law, and Dunnicott names the exceptions before anybody asks: the bag of curtain hooks on the same trestle since ten, the coat that came in at four and went in eleven minutes” — and the sentence after it reasserts the pattern’s force, since being ‘wrong about one in four’ means right three times in four. That concession-then-reassertion turn is exactly ‘Still’. B fails because ‘Granted’ introduces the concession, and the concession has already been made in the previous sentence; putting it before the reassertion reverses the polarity. C asserts a consequence, but the exceptions do not cause her accuracy — they cut against it. D is merely temporal and leaves the exceptions unanswered, which the paragraph plainly is answering.

Fenniscarth says it directly: “the plasticiser that kept it soft has soaked into the paper. Where the glue went in, the sheet’s gone like greased paper; you can read the back through it” — that is C, adhesive migrating into the sheet and leaving it translucent. A swaps the chemistry the quote separates: “The rubber in it has oxidised – that’s the brown”, so the brown is oxidised rubber, while the plasticiser is what soaked in and made the paper translucent. B reverses the treatments: “She warms a mend from last year, and the film lifts … On one like this, heat does nothing. The glue has gone hard, so only a solvent will move it” — heat is for the still-soft mend, solvent for the hardened one. D overreaches her own hedge: “The brown that’s in the fibres I can lighten. I don’t promise to take it out”, and the solvent-matching remark applies to shifting the glue, not to clearing the stain.

The rule is stated — “The second fortnight needed no asking” and was free until “the twenty-ninth day, when a penny a day began” — and so is the only thing that ended it: “What stopped the second fortnight was the slate by the door, where a subscriber set down the title he wanted; a volume so claimed came in on the fourteenth day.” Since keeping a book a second fortnight cost nothing and required no permission, a fourteenth-day return signals a claim on the slate. The travels came in on the fourteenth day 39 times out of 41, so subscribers were repeatedly giving it up at the fortnight with another reader waiting — a conclusion recoverable from the ledger even though “The slate was rubbed clean every week and no copy of it was kept.” That is A. B contradicts the charging rule: continuation ran to day 28 free, and the sermons were “continued seven times” within that window, so no penny a day arose. C misreads “Fifty-three subscribers paid a guinea a year, and three of them chose what was bought” — three individuals selected, with no meeting and no vote of the membership. D is contradicted by “Eleven of the fifty-three paid their guinea in each of the nine years and carried nothing home”: they kept paying through the whole run of the ledger, 1827 to 1835.

Texten anger tidpunkten på ett ställe: “buföringen dit bestämdes på byastämman: djuren fick inte gå upp innan löven var utslagna, och den som drog i väg för tidigt fick böta” — alltså både stämmans beslut och lövsprickningen, vilket är precis C, med böterna som belagg för att beslutet var bindande. A blandar ihop två saker: höet förklarar varför djuren över huvud taget fördes bort (“Inägorna … behövdes till vinterfodret, och en ko som betade på hemängen i juli åt upp det hö hon skulle leva på i februari”), inte när buföringen skedde, och någon mätning av kvarvarande hö nämns aldrig. B tar en uppgift ur fel stycke: “männen och de äldre kvinnorna behövdes hemma till slåttern” förklarar vilka som följde med, inte när man drog i väg. D nämner snö och is som texten aldrig berör; enda naturtecknet som anges är löven.

Kontrasten står utskriven: om ropen gäller att “En ko gick mot den röst hon kände igen, och två kvinnor på samma vall lockade därför inte lika; den som var ny måste börja med att lära djuren att känna igen just hennes rop”, medan “Med hornet var det tvärtom. Dess signaler var få och bestämda … tre stötar betydde att någon behövde hjälp.” Det är D: ropen var personliga, hornsignalerna hade fast innebörd. A vänder på en detalj — “en stilla kväll” sägs om hornet (“De hördes till Klintbodarna och en stilla kväll ända ned till byn”), inte om ropen, och blåst nämns aldrig. B hittar på en tidsuppdelning: ropen användes om kvällen (“lockades djuren hem om kvällen”), inte i gryningen, och hornet i dimma var ett undantag som suddade gränsen, inte en kvällsregel. C:s rovdjur förekommer inte i texten alls; hornets signaler “riktade sig till människor”.

Lönen beskrivs i ett svep: “Fäbodfolket lejdes för en sommar i taget, och lönen gjordes upp i maj, innan buföringen: till större delen varor – skor, vadmal, en tunna korn – och en mindre summa pengar som betalades ut på hösten”, med exemplet Blenda Nyholm 1897 “med sex kronor, ett par skor och tre alnar vadmal”. Avtalad på våren, mest i varor — det är A. B förutsätter en resultatdel som texten inte har: lönen “gjordes upp i maj, innan buföringen”, alltså innan något smör eller någon ost fanns att mäta. C stannar vid halva meningen — penningdelen betalades på hösten, men varorna var avtalade och inget kopplas till någon försäljning; texten nämner över huvud taget ingen försäljning av fäbodvarorna. D motsägs direkt av “lejdes för en sommar i taget” och av “Den som hade skött en vall väl kunde välja gård nästa år”.

Avståndet och hållbarheten bär hela texten och binder ihop annars skilda avsnitt: “allt som skulle bäras hem måste först göras hållbart” i inledningen, “Vad som gjordes av mjölken bestämdes av hur varan skulle klara buföringen och färden ned” med osten som torkades desto mer ju längre bort fäboden låg, “Avståndet överbryggades också med ljud”, och slutsättningen om mejeriet: “Fäbodens idé hade varit den motsatta: avståndet betydde litet så länge varan tålde att vänta. Nu satte avståndet i stället priset.” Det är B. A täcker bara ett stycke — vallkullorna — och lämnar både mjölkhanteringen och avvecklingen utanför. C täcker bara de två senare styckena om mejeriföreningen 1904 och Pilhammars sammanställning, och missar hela första halvan. D täcker bara stycke två om inägor och utmark, alltså förutsättningen för bruket, inte det som texten följer genom året och genom avvecklingen.

Arithmetic, worked two ways, and both give sixteen. The reference class is fixed by “Alla som vill stå måste söka varje år” — everyone who wants a stall, incumbent or newcomer, applies every year — so “Sjuttiofyra sökte plats till den marknaden” is the whole application pool, not a newcomers-only pool. Route one: 74 applicants against a hard ceiling of 58, since “Torget rymmer femtioåtta stånd och fler får inte plats” and “alla femtioåtta stånd var upptagna när den öppnade”, gives 74 − 58 = 16 left without. Route two goes through the priority rule: “den som stod på torget året innan får stå där igen”, and “Fyra platser blev lediga” means 54 of the 58 incumbents returned, so 74 − 54 = 20 non-incumbent applicants chased 4 vacancies and 20 − 4 = 16 were turned away. The two routes converge, so the passage now fixes the answer unambiguously; the only reading that would break it — taking the 74 as new applicants disjoint from the 54 returners, which would give 70 — is foreclosed by “Alla som vill stå måste söka varje år” and by the unqualified “sökte plats till den marknaden”. A is contradicted by that same priority rule: places are not drawn by lot, incumbents keep theirs. B misapplies the four from “Fyra platser blev lediga” to plats 1, which is the one place the text says has not changed hands — “står i Gottfrid Runessons namn och har gjort det längre än platskartan går tillbaka”. C reverses the priority rule outright.

The writer’s position is stated as an imperative — “Flytta hela marknaden, båda dagarna, från och med nästa höst” — and she accepts the cost of it: “De första åren blir sämre. Ingen som räknar kommer fram till något annat, och jag tänker inte påstå att det ordnar sig av sig självt.” That is A: move, and bear the worse years. B is contradicted by “båda dagarna” in the same sentence, and the one-day option is what she describes as the majority’s objection (“Den som står ensam kan inte stå två dagar”), not her proposal. C confuses her acknowledgement with her conclusion — she writes “De trettionio har två skäl, och båda håller” and “Det svaret har jag inte”, yet she was “en av de tolv” and still argues for moving. D is refused explicitly: “Ett provår vill jag ändå inte ha … eftersom folk måste hinna vänja sig vid att åka dit.”

Kriteriet står utskrivet och är negativt avgränsat: “Vem som fick komma in avgjordes inte av hur nära man stod varandra, utan av vad besöket gällde. Prästen släpptes in, och distriktssköterskan, och karlen som skulle värdera skogen. De kom i ärenden som rörde hushållet” — det är A ordagrant. B motsägs av samma mening plus “Grannar och släkt satt i köket, oavsett hur långt de hade rest” och “Den som stod hushållet närmast kom sällan längre än till köksbordet”. C faller på “Sköterskan var oanmäld varannan gång och visades in ändå”, som är insatt just för att slå undan föranmälan som kriterium. D är det närmaste alternativet men byter ut ärendet mot rang: texten anger ärendet som det avgörande (“De kom i ärenden som rörde hushållet och tog med sig ett omdöme därifrån”), och gränsen går inte vid aktning — Lars Uddén i huset intill blir stående i farstun inte för att han skattas lågt utan för att han inte kommer i något ärende.

Slutsatsen bärs av Hildings citat: teven stod i finrummet i tre vintrar, “de satt i ytterrock framför den” och “Man frös och man såg på”, tills “Sen bar far ut den i köket, för där gick spisen ändå”, varefter “Dörren till finrummet gick igen som förut” — tittandet, och därmed kvällarna, hamnade i köket dit apparaten till slut flyttades. Det är C. A låter rimlig på Hildings “Samma soffgrupp står kvar hos honom”, men motsägs av berättarens egen mening: “Hemma hos oss stod farfars kista i finrummet flera år efter att vår apparat hade burits ut” — rummet användes alltså vidare för sitt tyngsta ändamål, så “orört” håller inte. B motsägs av just “Samma soffgrupp står kvar hos honom”: möblerna byttes inte ut. D bryter mot tidsuppgiften “i tre vintrar innan huset fick element”, varefter den bars ut — inte över tio år.

The book's dace total is set against the netting in one span: “Over fifteen springs the book records 6,140 brown trout, 288 grayling, 31 dace and nine chub”, then “one afternoon’s netting last May took four hundred-odd of them, more than the trap has held in fifteen years” – fifteen years being the whole life of the book, since “Since the pass opened in 2011 the trap has been emptied most mornings of the run, the counts written into a hardbacked book”, so 'ever' and 'in fifteen years' coincide and B is literally true. A fails on that same span twice: 1931 is when “a mill that stopped in 1931” stopped, and the counts begin with the pass in 2011, not 1931. D inverts “The first nine springs are in one hand, the rest in three others” – one keeper wrote the first nine springs, three wrote the rest, not three of four writing the first nine. C invents a mis-identification of chub as dace; the text never questions the determinations, it only reports totals, and the argument it does build about dace turns on route, not on recording error.

“Of 74 tagged, 61 reached the weir, 54 on the left, and 39 went into the pass … Twelve came out at the top” – 27 of the 39 entrants failed, so most that entered did not reach the top pool, which is D. A is refuted by the split Kelsingham draws: “Of the eleven that entered above ten degrees, seven got out; of the twenty-eight that entered colder, five did” – 7/11 against 5/28 is not doing about as well, and the whole paragraph exists to mark the contrast (she calls it “suggestive and no more”, which qualifies the inference, not the disparity). B is contradicted head-on by “The pools do not help. They are short, and at April flows the jet from one notch reaches the wall of the next; there is no quiet corner in them.” C picks the wrong attribute: the obstacle named is build, not size – “A grayling is deep through the body and carries a dorsal fin like a sail, and it does not leave the water” – and size is the term applied to the dace (“a dace is a small fish”) in the strength account she rejects.

Kelsingham's own summary is the key span: “They don’t find it, and they don’t find it because they don’t come up that side of the river”, expanded by “they move up in loose shoals along the margins, and the right margin is a long slack behind a shingle bar. A fish that follows it arrives on the far side from the entrance, thirty metres of broken water away”, plus the attraction-flow arithmetic “The pass releases about a quarter of a cubic metre a second; in April the river brings down nine. Four metres out from the mouth there is nothing of that quarter left to follow.” A states exactly those two halves – wrong bank, and too little flow to draw them across. B is the explanation the text raises in order to dismiss: “The explanation people reach for first is strength … the fall from one pool to the next about 270 millimetres … Kelsingham … thinks strength has little to do with it”, and “The dace aren’t beaten by the ladder.” C invents a timing mismatch found nowhere; the trap is emptied “most mornings of the run” and 174 tagged dace reached the weir within nine days, so they arrive while the pass is working. D misuses the shoal detail: shoaling is cited to explain which margin they travel, not any refusal to enter a channel singly – nine did go in and five came out.

The two orifices are distinguished by one controlled variable: “A spate in February packed the lower one to the top with gravel, and it is still packed. The other, three walls further up, came through the same water clear.” ‘The same water’ explicitly holds the event constant, so the only difference left in the text is height in the pass, which is what C infers. That same phrase is what kills A: if both met the same spate and one survived, the passage gives no ground for calling the spate unusually heavy, and it never grades the February flow against a normal year. B misstates purpose against the stated one – they were cut “so a fish could go through a wall instead of over it”, a passage route, not a way of bleeding water out of the notches. D asserts a result the text withholds: the upper orifice is reported clear, not used; the only fish numbers anywhere are the book counts and Kelsingham's two springs of tagging, both predating 2023, so nothing licenses a claim that fish have been getting through it.

The article's spine is one pass and three outcomes with two different diagnoses. Trout succeed – “a trout goes up without appearing to try”, 6,140 in the book; dace fail outside the structure – “They don’t find it … because they don’t come up that side of the river”; grayling fail inside it – “39 went into the pass … Twelve came out at the top. Whatever stops them is inside”, with “Kelsingham keeps them apart” flagging that the two cases are not the same case. D names that structure. C is the closing paragraph only – the second mouth she recommends and the 2023 orifices – and inverts emphasis, since the piece is diagnosis first and remedy last. A is off-target: what the weir holds back is the premise, and the river above is barely discussed; the text's interest is stated as “Nobody says the pass does not work … what it works for.” B smuggles in a methodological thesis the text never argues, and gets the evidence backwards: the trap counts are precisely what the article treats as insufficient (“the book counts only what went through the trap”, and the trout run in winters when the weir drowns out), the load being carried instead by tags and antennas.

“A jacket that would have ___ two pounds at half past ten goes at three for whatever coin is held out”: the subject is the goods and the complement is a price, which is the fixed collocation 'fetch a price' – D. The parallel verb in the same sentence, 'goes at three for whatever coin', confirms that the frame is the item realising a sum, not an agent being paid. A 'earned' takes an animate earner or an investment that works for its return; a jacket on a trestle does neither, and 'earned two pounds' would credit the jacket with effort the sentence denies it. B 'gained' means increased by / acquired for itself, so 'gained two pounds' reads as the jacket becoming two pounds heavier or richer – the wrong argument structure for a selling price. C 'returned' needs an invested outlay to be returned on, and the piece's whole premise is donated jumble, priced at a saucer of coins with no cost base – “The saucers of coins go to one end of the trestle”.

“Whether the hall is worth ___ open for a last hour”: 'worth' as a predicative adjective governs a gerund, so 'worth keeping open' – C. This is a pure structural gap and the three competitors fail on form alone. A 'keep' would be a bare infinitive, which 'worth' never licenses. B 'kept' gives a past participle, which would need a passive frame the sentence does not supply ('the hall is worth kept open' is ungrammatical). D 'to keep' is the classic learner substitution – 'worth' is the one adjective in this family that refuses the to-infinitive, unlike 'able to' or 'ready to' – and 'worth to keep open' is ungrammatical in every register of English.

The gap sits in a change-of-state frame after the prices are abolished: “At four the prices come off … nothing has a price after that, and the afternoon moves from a sale to a ___”. Since the contrast term is 'a sale', the filler must be something that is not a sale, and 'nothing has a price' plus Dunnicott's “Nobody’s buying after four … They’re doing us a favour” fixes it as free distribution – giveaway, B. A 'clearance' is a species of sale with reduced prices, so it collapses the contrast the sentence is built on, and would also be false of a table where nothing is priced. C 'markdown' names a price reduction, which again presupposes prices; the text says they ‘come off’ entirely, not down. D 'liquidation' is both a sale and the wrong register – it belongs to a business winding up its assets, whereas this is a village hall jumble whose leftovers are being carried away as a favour.

The gap explains why late-arriving goods are unsold: “Boxes come in all day, and the ones that arrive after two are the ones their owners have been circling all week … Those are on the trestles at five not because the village refused them but because they were ___ offered”, glossed immediately by “What is left at that hour is sorted by arrival time at least as much as by taste.” The variable is exposure time, so 'briefly' – B. A 'amply' asserts generous supply, which neither answers 'not because the village refused them' nor connects to arrival time. C 'thinly' would describe sparse spreading of a substance or of numbers, not the duration of an offer, and clashes with goods described as the best of the day. D 'openly' introduces a concealment contrast the piece never raises – the items are on open trestles in a public hall; nothing suggests they were hidden, whereas the sorting-by-arrival-time sentence is a direct paraphrase of 'briefly'.

The preceding sentence is the concession – “The pattern is not a law, and Dunnicott names the exceptions before anybody asks: the bag of curtain hooks on the same trestle since ten, the coat that came in at four and went in eleven minutes” – and the gap opens the reassertion that survives it: “___, she can walk the tables at five and say which hour a thing came in, and be wrong about one in four.” That is concessive-then-nevertheless, so 'Still' – A. B 'Granted' points the wrong way: it opens a concession, but the concession has just been made in the previous sentence, and its slot is now occupied. C 'Therefore' claims the exceptions entail the skill, which reverses the logic – exceptions weaken a pattern, they do not license it. D 'Afterwards' is temporal sequencing, but nothing here happens after the curtain hooks and the coat; both are standing examples inside the same five-o'clock scene the gap sentence describes.

Fenniscarth's account of what the adhesive does to the sheet is verbatim: “the plasticiser that kept it soft has soaked into the paper. Where the glue went in, the sheet’s gone like greased paper; you can read the back through it” – translucency where the adhesive penetrates, which is C. A swaps the two components of her chemistry: “The rubber in it has oxidised – that’s the brown”, so the stain is oxidised rubber; the plasticiser is the migrating softener, and the brown band is described on the certificate whose film is still partly present (“Three flakes of film clung along one edge”), not as something dated from the film's departure. B reverses her two treatments: “She warms a mend from last year, and the film lifts and brings most of the glue with it. On one like this, heat does nothing. The glue has gone hard, so only a solvent will move it” – heat for the still-soft recent mend, solvent for the hardened one. D overstates her explicitly hedged limit: “About the stain itself she is careful: ‘The brown that’s in the fibres I can lighten. I don’t promise to take it out.’”

The rule and the numbers interlock. The rule: “The second fortnight needed no asking … What stopped the second fortnight was the slate by the door, where a subscriber set down the title he wanted; a volume so claimed came in on the fourteenth day.” The numbers: “A book of travels went out 41 times in those nine years; 39 of the loans came in on the fourteenth day, and two were continued.” Since keeping a book a second fortnight cost nothing and required no asking, a day-fourteen return is the signature of a slate claim, so on 39 of 41 loans the travels was surrendered at the fortnight with another subscriber waiting – A, and the sermons contrast (“out nine times and was continued seven times”) is there to show the same rule producing the opposite pattern when nobody claims. B misreads the tariff: “nothing was charged before the twenty-ninth day, when a penny a day began”, and a continuation is the second fortnight, days fifteen to twenty-eight, so the seven continued sermon loans were free. C invents a meeting and the wrong body: “Fifty-three subscribers paid a guinea a year, and three of them chose what was bought” – selection sat with three people, not with a subscribers' vote. D contradicts the span given: “Eleven of the fifty-three paid their guinea in each of the nine years and carried nothing home” – they went on paying through the ledger's last year, which is the point of the sentence.

Tidpunkten regleras i en enda mening: “Fyra gårdar i Ryttmo delade på Trindbodarna … och buföringen dit bestämdes på byastämman: djuren fick inte gå upp innan löven var utslagna, och den som drog i väg för tidigt fick böta.” Alltså två saker, precis som C: stämmans beslut och lövsprickningen. A tar fel storhet – höet styr varför djuren måste bort (“en ko som betade på hemängen i juli åt upp det hö hon skulle leva på i februari”), inte när de gick; texten nämner aldrig kvarvarande hö i ladorna som en signal. B blandar ihop bemanning med almanacka: slåttern förklarar vilka som stannade hemma (“männen och de äldre kvinnorna behövdes hemma till slåttern”), inte när buföringen skedde. D för in snösmältning och islössning som inte finns i texten alls; den enda naturliga markören som anges är lövsprickningen, och den enda datumangivelsen är “från mitten av juni till mikaelitiden”.

Kontrasten står utskriven: om kulningen heter det “Ropen var ändå inte signaler i egentlig mening. En ko gick mot den röst hon kände igen, och två kvinnor på samma vall lockade därför inte lika; den som var ny måste börja med att lära djuren att känna igen just hennes rop”, och om hornet “Med hornet var det tvärtom. Dess signaler var få och bestämda … tre stötar betydde att någon behövde hjälp.” Det är D: personberoende rop mot fast innebörd. A hänger på ett halvcitat – “en stilla kväll” gäller hornets räckvidd ned till byn, inte ropens, och blåst ställs aldrig mot något; texten jämför i stället räckvidd rakt av (“längre än något rop bar”). B har fel tider: ropen användes på kvällen (“med den lockades djuren hem om kvällen”), och hornet i dimma – men dimman är ett undantag som suddar gränsen (“hornet användes också för att samla djuren i dimma”), inte en tidsangivelse. C hittar på rovdjur; hornets angivna adressat är människor – “riktade sig till människor”.

Löneformen står i klartext: “Fäbodfolket lejdes för en sommar i taget, och lönen gjordes upp i maj, innan buföringen: till större delen varor – skor, vadmal, en tunna korn – och en mindre summa pengar som betalades ut på hösten”, med exemplet “Blenda Nyholm uppförd för sommaren 1897 med sex kronor, ett par skor och tre alnar vadmal”. Det är A: avtalad på våren (maj), mest in natura. B inför ackord på producerad mängd; lönen är tvärtom uppgjord i förväg, innan en enda ost är gjord, och det enda som knyter skicklighet till utfall är valfriheten nästa år (“Den som hade skött en vall väl kunde välja gård nästa år”), inte beloppet. C gör penningdelens hösttermin till ett försäljningsvillkor; texten säger när den betalades, inte att den hängde på att varorna sålts, och varorna fördes hem till gårdarna. D motsägs direkt av “för en sommar i taget”.

Texten är byggd kring avstånd och hållbarhet, och säger det själv tre gånger: “En fäbod låg där den låg därför att betet fanns där, och allt som skulle bäras hem måste först göras hållbart”; “Vad som gjordes av mjölken bestämdes av hur varan skulle klara buföringen och färden ned … ju längre bort från byn en fäbod låg, desto torrare gjordes de”; och i vändpunkten “Fäbodens idé hade varit den motsatta: avståndet betydde litet så länge varan tålde att vänta. Nu satte avståndet i stället priset.” Även kulningsstycket ingår (“Avståndet överbryggades också med ljud”). B täcker alltså hela bågen. A täcker ett stycke om arbetskraften. C täcker avvecklingen – mejeriet och Pilhammar – men lämnar buföring, tillverkning, ljud och nutid utanför, och mejeriet förklaras dessutom just genom avståndet. D täcker inägor mot utmark, det vill säga ett stycke som texten själv avfärdar som “lätt att förklara” innan den går vidare till det som bär resten.

Räkningen går ihop och referensklassen är nu låst. Tre spann bär den: “Torget rymmer femtioåtta stånd och fler får inte plats”, “Alla som vill stå måste söka varje år, men den som stod på torget året innan får stå där igen”, och “Fyra platser blev lediga inför förra höstens marknad. Sjuttiofyra sökte plats till den marknaden, och alla femtioåtta stånd var upptagna när den öppnade.” Eftersom varje sökande som fick plats är ett av de 58 upptagna stånden, och varje upptaget stånd måste ha sökts, blir 74 − 58 = 16 utan plats. Den konkurrerande läsningen ger samma tal: om de 74 delas i 54 återvändande (58 − 4 lediga) och 20 nya som slåss om de fyra lediga, blir 20 − 4 = 16. Den enda läsning som ger ett annat tal – att de 74 vore enbart nya sökande, alltså 70 utan plats – stängs av “Alla som vill stå måste söka varje år”, som uttryckligen räknar in de sittande i sökandeskaran (skribenten själv är sittande, “plats 42 på torget”), och delsumman “alla femtioåtta stånd var upptagna” utesluter tomma platser som annars skulle höja talet. A motsägs av samma företrädesregel – ingen lottning nämns, och förtur är motsatsen till lott. B saknar stöd: “Plats 1 … står i Gottfrid Runessons namn och har gjort det längre än platskartan går tillbaka” beskriver ingen enda bytt innehavare, än mindre fyra; fyran kommer från de lediga platserna. C vänder regeln baklänges. Talet 43 (“Fyrtiotre av de femtioåtta stånden … sköts av en enda människa”) hör till tvådagarsargumentet och ger ingen alternativ subtraktion.

Skribenten deklarerar sin ståndpunkt två gånger och avvisar uttryckligen mellanlägena: “Flytta hela marknaden, båda dagarna, från och med nästa höst”, och om övergången “De första åren blir sämre. Ingen som räknar kommer fram till något annat, och jag tänker inte påstå att det ordnar sig av sig självt.” Att hon ändå vill flytta är just “tåla de sämre åren” – A. B står i direkt strid med “båda dagarna”; endagsalternativet är motpartens problembild (“Den som står ensam kan inte stå två dagar”), ett skäl hon medger utan svar men inte antar. C är motsatsen till hennes röst: “Jag var en av de tolv”, alltså av dem som ville flytta ut. D avvisas ordagrant: “Ett provår vill jag ändå inte ha. Att stå ett år på fältet och sedan flytta tillbaka lär ingen någonting, eftersom folk måste hinna vänja sig vid att åka dit.”

Kriteriet står utskrivet i satsen som inleder stycket: “Vem som fick komma in avgjordes inte av hur nära man stod varandra, utan av vad besöket gällde”, med exempellistan “Prästen släpptes in, och distriktssköterskan, och karlen som skulle värdera skogen. De kom i ärenden som rörde hushållet.” Det är A ordagrant. B är den läsning texten uttryckligen förnekar och sedan illustrerar mot: “Grannar och släkt satt i köket, oavsett hur långt de hade rest … Den som stod hushållet närmast kom sällan längre än till köksbordet”, och Lars Uddén från huset intill blev stående i farstun. C motsägs av “Sköterskan var oanmäld varannan gång och visades in ändå”. D byter kriteriet från ärende till rang; texten graderar aldrig gäster efter aktning, och de insläppta beskrivs snarare som utifrånkommande bedömare – “De kom i ärenden som rörde hushållet och tog med sig ett omdöme därifrån” – medan de man höll kärast satt i köket.

Teven flyttar och tittandet flyttar med den: “Hos Hilding Wibbelund stod den i tre vintrar innan huset fick element, och de satt i ytterrock framför den … ’Sen bar far ut den i köket, för där gick spisen ändå.’ Dörren till finrummet gick igen som förut.” Skälet – att spisen gick i köket – och den återstängda dörren ger just C: kvällarna hamnade i köket dit apparaten till slut flyttades. A låter sig inte dras, eftersom rummet bevisligen användes efteråt: “Hemma hos oss stod farfars kista i finrummet flera år efter att vår apparat hade burits ut”, vilket är motsatsen till orört. B motsägs av “Samma soffgrupp står kvar hos honom” – möblerna byttes inte ut. D spräcker tidsangivelsen: “tre vintrar” i rummet, varefter den bars ut; tio år finns ingenstans, och de ’flera år’ som nämns gäller kistan efter utbärningen, inte apparatens tid i finrummet.
